valley.drawingAlt: Lily pads on a still pond. On each pad, the frogs sing one song.
locals: I hop to a pad where they sing my song. One or two like me, that is all I want.
Each pad sings one song now. Nobody planned it.
Pell sings the old song alone, the one with all the parts.

notes.title: Small wishes, big walls
notes.science: Frogs that want only a few neighbors like them still end up on pads of one song. Small wishes add up to big walls.
notes.limits: Frogs are not people, and a song is not who you are. Models like this one predict more sorting than real cities show.
notes.counter: Real segregation also has causes this pond leaves out: laws, lending, jobs, and money. People built many of those walls on purpose.
notes.question: What did each frog want, and what did the pond get?

sources.label: Parable of the Polygons, Vi Hart and Nicky Case
Dynamic Models of Segregation, Thomas Schelling, 1971
Understanding the Social Context of the Schelling Segregation Model, Clark and Fossett, 2008
The Color of Law, Richard Rothstein, 2017

notes.title: A second song
notes.science: A frog that knows two songs fits on more pads. In the model, a small wish for some variety takes the walls down again.
notes.limits: Learning a song is fast here. In a real town, change is slower.
notes.counter: Some groups keep their song on purpose, to keep it alive.
notes.question: Whose song did you learn?
